explain: Further losses of about 10-15% occur in transmission and distribution on the grid. Cogeneration tackles the problem by using heat that would otherwise be rejected.

front: What are the macro-level and micro-level benefits of cogeneration?
back: Macro: it shares part of the national utility's financial burden with the private sector and conserves indigenous energy sources. Micro: it can cut a user's overall energy bill, especially where power and heat are needed together and tariffs are rational.
explain: At the national level, cogeneration spreads the investment burden. At site level, the saving depends on having a simultaneous need for both power and heat.

front: Why does on-site cogeneration reduce the burden on the utility network?
back: Electricity is generated on-site, so the grid carries less load and the transmission line losses are eliminated.
explain: Cogeneration also saves fossil fuel and reduces greenhouse gas emissions, particularly CO₂.

front: Name the three cogeneration technologies that have been widely commercialised.
back: (1) Extraction or back-pressure steam turbines. (2) Gas turbine with heat recovery boiler, with or without a bottoming steam turbine. (3) Reciprocating engines with heat recovery boiler.
explain: These three are the mainstream options. The chapter then describes each one in turn, with its heat-to-power characteristics.

front: What is a specific advantage of steam turbines over other prime movers in cogeneration?
back: They can burn a wide range of fuels, including coal, natural gas, fuel oil and biomass.
explain: Some power generation efficiency may be given up to optimise heat supply. Steam turbines are mostly used where electricity demand is above 1 MW, up to a few hundred MW.

front: Why are back-pressure cogeneration plants free of the need for large cooling towers?
back: Their exhaust steam is used by the process, so there is no large condensing system to reject leftover heat.
explain: Condensing turbines need a condenser and cooling tower to reject the heat that is not used. Back-pressure plants avoid that equipment.

front: What size range do gas turbines cover in cogeneration, and which fuel is most common?
back: From a fraction of a MW to about 100 MW. Natural gas is the most common fuel; light fuel oil or diesel can also be used.
explain: Gas turbine cogeneration has grown fast because of natural gas availability, shorter project gestation and modular delivery.

front: What is the main trade-off of gas turbine cogeneration between heat and power?
back: Low heat-to-power conversion efficiency, but more heat can be recovered at higher temperatures.
explain: The high-temperature exhaust suits a wide range of heating and cooling uses. Gas turbines also have a short start-up time and can run intermittently.

front: How can a gas turbine cogeneration unit boost its heat output when the site needs more heat?
back: Supplementary natural gas firing: extra fuel is mixed into the oxygen-rich exhaust gas and burned.
explain: The exhaust still holds oxygen, so the extra firing raises thermal output efficiently. Many large units use this to change their heat-to-power ratio.

front: Why are reciprocating engines popular with smaller energy-consuming facilities?
back: They have high power generation efficiency, their heat recovery is efficient at small sizes, and they suit sites that need more electricity than heat, where low-quality heat (low-pressure steam or hot water) is acceptable.
explain: Reciprocating engines are ideal for intermittent operation. Their performance is not as sensitive to ambient temperature as that of gas turbines.

front: True or false: reciprocating engine performance is more sensitive to ambient temperature than gas turbine performance.
back: False. Engine performance is not as sensitive to ambient temperature changes as gas turbine performance.
explain: The drawback of engines is cost, not temperature sensitivity: a low initial investment, but high operating and maintenance costs from wear and tear.

front: Name the four types of topping cycle cogeneration.
back: (1) Combined-cycle topping: gas turbine, then heat recovery boiler, then steam turbine. (2) Steam-turbine topping: high-pressure boiler steam through a turbine, with low-pressure exhaust for process. (3) Diesel or gas engine with heat recovery from exhaust and jacket water. (4) Gas-turbine topping: gas turbine drives a generator and its exhaust feeds a heat recovery boiler.
explain: In a topping cycle the fuel makes power first, and the leftover heat is the by-product used for process heat. Topping cycles are the most popular form of cogeneration.

front: Which industries mainly use bottoming-cycle cogeneration, and why?
back: Cement, steel, ceramic, gas and petrochemical industries, where high-temperature furnace or kiln heat is rejected at significantly high temperatures.
explain: The rejected heat drives a recovery boiler and turbine-generator to make power. Bottoming-cycle plants are much less common than topping-cycle plants.

front: In base electrical load matching, how is the plant sized and how is the rest of the power supplied?
back: It is sized to the site's minimum electricity demand, taken from the historical demand curve. The rest of the power is bought from the grid.
explain: Thermal demand can be met by the cogeneration system alone or with additional boilers. Surplus heat can be exported to neighbouring customers if the situation permits.

front: In base thermal load matching, how is the plant sized and what covers extra demand?
back: It is sized to the minimum thermal requirement and runs at full load at all times. Standby boilers or burners supply the extra heat, and extra power is bought from the grid.
explain: If local law permits, excess electricity can be sold to the power utility.

front: Which operating scheme makes a facility a stand-alone system, independent of the utility grid?
back: Electrical load matching.
explain: The system must cover all site power needs, including reserves for scheduled and unscheduled maintenance. Auxiliary boilers meet any extra heat demand, and surplus heat is wasted unless it can be exported.

front: In thermal load matching, what does the plant follow, and how are power deficits and surpluses handled?
back: It follows the site's heat demand at any time. A power shortfall is bought from the grid, and excess electricity can be sold to the utility if local legislation permits.
explain: The prime movers are operated according to the thermal demand, so electricity output is set by the heat requirement.

front: Which cogeneration system has the widest heat-to-power ratio range, and what is it?
back: Back-pressure steam turbine, 4.0 to 14.3. For comparison: extraction-condensing steam turbine 2.0 to 10.0; gas turbine 1.3 to 2.0; combined cycle 1.0 to 1.7; reciprocating engine 1.1 to 2.5.
explain: The steam turbine offers a large range of heat-to-power ratios, which is why it fits many different sites. Both heat and power are expressed in the same unit (kW) for the ratio.

front: Under what three conditions is cogeneration most attractive?
back: (a) Steam and power demand are balanced, within the steam-to-power output range of a suitable plant. (b) One plant or a group of plants has enough steam and power demand for economies of scale. (c) Peaks and troughs in demand can be managed, or adequate utility backup is available for electricity.
explain: These conditions link the heat-to-power ratio to the load-matching schemes. Electricity backup is what allows a plant to cover demand peaks.

front: Why does a sugar mill (heat at about 120 °C) suit a topping cycle, while a cement plant (heat at about 1450 °C) suits a bottoming cycle?
back: Lower-temperature heat, such as a sugar mill's 120 °C, fits a topping cycle. Very high-temperature heat, such as a cement plant's 1450 °C, fits a bottoming cycle, which also supplies electricity.
explain: The required quality of thermal energy (temperature and pressure) decides the type of cogeneration system.

front: Why is a rice mill a good candidate for steam turbine cogeneration?
back: It needs mechanical power for milling and heat for paddy drying, and a steam turbine can burn rice husk, the mill's own waste product.
explain: Cheap fuels or waste products often decide whether a cogeneration option is competitive, because they set the running cost.

front: Why should cogeneration for a pulp and paper plant be modular?
back: The plant cannot run long without process steam, so the system should have more than one unit. If one unit shuts down, the energy supply is not seriously affected.
explain: Modularity is a reliability feature for sites that cannot tolerate a prolonged loss of heat or power.

front: How does a grid-dependent cogeneration system differ from a grid-independent (stand-alone) one?
back: A grid-dependent system can buy or sell electricity through the grid. A stand-alone system meets all of the site's energy demands by itself.
explain: For the same facility, the technical configuration differs between the two designs, so the choice must be made early.

front: How can local environmental regulations limit the cogeneration choice?
back: Stringent rules can rule out some fuels, because the cost of treating polluted exhaust gas, or of treating the fuel itself, can be too high.
explain: Environmental rules therefore affect the technology and fuel choice, not only emissions limits.

front: What overall thermal efficiency can a back-pressure cogeneration system reach with an efficient boiler?
back: As much as 90%, when all the exhaust steam is used. The only other losses are gear drive, generator and steam generation.
explain: The chapter's notes on cogeneration efficiency quote up to 85% for back-pressure systems. Both figures appear in the book, so use the number the question asks for.

front: Compared with a back-pressure turbine, what does an extraction-condensing turbine offer, and what does it cost?
back: A higher power-to-heat ratio and higher electricity generation efficiency. The cost is a lower overall thermal efficiency, because exhaust heat is lost in the cooling water.
explain: Condensing systems need more auxiliary equipment, such as the condenser and cooling towers. They suit sites where electricity demand is much higher than steam demand and the load fluctuates.

front: What temperatures apply to gas turbine gases at inlet and exhaust, and why is the exhaust useful?
back: Gases enter at 900-1000 °C and leave at about 450-550 °C. The book gives 400-500 °C for the exit in one place. The hot exhaust makes the gas turbine well suited to high-grade heat supply.
explain: The exhaust can meet all or part of the site's thermal (steam) demand. The OCR of the chapter shows the exit range twice with slightly different numbers.

front: Which fuels suit gas turbines, and why must the hot gas be clean?
back: Natural gas is most used. Gas oil, LPG and naphtha are also suitable. The hot gas must be free of particulates that erode the blades and of contaminants that cause corrosion.
explain: A gas turbine runs at high speed and high temperature, so high-premium fuels are preferred. Distillate oils such as gas oil are also used.

front: What is the efficiency of a stand-alone gas turbine without any heat recovery system?
back: About 35 to 40%.
explain: Losses come from blade efficiency, leakage through clearance spaces, friction and turbulence. Heat recovery in a steam generator is what recovers much of the rest.

front: What share of the turbine's generated energy does the air compressor consume, and what does that do to net efficiency?
back: About 50 to 60%. The 35-40% figures exclude the compressor, fuel pump and other auxiliaries, so the net turbine efficiency is lower than the calculated figure.
explain: In most gas turbine plants the air compressor is an integral part of the turbine plant, so the net figure is the one that counts for usable output.

front: What is turbine heat rate, and in which units is it expressed?
back: The heat input to the turbine needed to produce 1 kWh of electricity. It is expressed in kJ/kWh (or kcal/kWh). 1 kWh = 3,600 kJ = 860 kcal.
explain: Heat rate and efficiency are inversely related only for a pure power plant. For cogeneration, the useful process heat is not counted in the heat rate, so the inverse does not apply.

front: What is a pressure survey on a steam turbine, and what conditions must it meet?
back: Pressure is noted at tapping points along the expansion path and compared with design values to infer the turbine's internal condition. The gauges must be accurate and the readings taken while the load is steady.
explain: A pressure survey should be carried out frequently on each running machine, because it shows deviations in performance early.

explain: The ratio compares useful thermal output with electrical output in the same unit (kW). Converting kJ/h to kW uses 1 kWh = 3,600 kJ.

front: What is trigeneration?
back: Simultaneous generation of steam (heat), power and refrigeration through integrated systems.
explain: Food processing and cold storage benefit most. A combined-cycle trigeneration plant with a gas turbine, waste heat boiler, steam turbine and absorption chiller can meet 100% of the facility's needs, with surplus power sold to the grid.

front: A chemical plant reduces steam from 17.6 kg/cm²(g) to 1.8 kg/cm²(g) through a PRV for a process needing 5,189 Mcal/h. Replacing the PRV with a back-pressure turbine (8,000 h/yr, fuel 10,000 kcal/kg at Rs 25/kg, grid power at Rs 6/kWh, gearbox 98%, alternator 98%, mechanical 97%, boiler 85%): what is the annual net saving?

With the same steam-to-power ratio and grid electricity at Rs 7/kWh, what is the daily saving from extra generation?

back: 750 kg/h of coal, which is 18,000 kg (18 tonnes) per day.
explain: The coal calculation uses the enthalpy rise from feed water to steam, divided by boiler efficiency and calorific value. It is the cost side of the extra power.

front: What is waste heat, and what matters more than its amount in a recovery study?
back: Waste heat is heat generated by fuel combustion or a chemical reaction that is dumped into the environment although it could still be reused economically. The essential quality of heat is its 'value', not its amount.
explain: The strategy for recovering heat depends partly on the temperature of the waste gases and on the economics involved. Two streams with the same heat content can have very different value, so temperature decides how practical recovery is.

front: Why is recovering heat from a high-temperature waste stream usually more cost-effective?
back: Higher temperature means higher quality heat, so recovery is usually more cost-effective.
explain: Heat at a higher temperature has more potential value for a useful purpose. Low-temperature waste heat generally needs a use that can accept it directly, such as space heating.

front: What must exist before any waste heat recovery study is worthwhile?
back: There must be some use for the recovered heat, such as preheating combustion air, space heating, or preheating boiler feed water or process water.
explain: The book stresses that recovered heat with no use is not a saving. Identify the sink for the heat before selecting any equipment.

front: What is a cascade system of waste heat recovery?
back: Recovery in stages: the high-temperature stage is used first (for example for air preheating), and the lower-temperature stage is used for process feed water heating or steam raising.
explain: Cascading matches each temperature level with a suitable use. This ensures the maximum amount of heat is recovered at the highest potential.

front: Flue gas from a heat treatment furnace leaves at 900 °C at 2,100 m³/h. It can be cooled to 180 °C. With density 1.19 kg/m³ and Cp 0.24 kcal/kg °C, how much heat is recoverable per hour, using Q = V × ρ × Cp × ΔT?
back: About 4,31,827 kcal/h.
explain: This is the book's worked example of the heat content formula. Only the temperature drop is recoverable, and Cp is per kg, so the volume flow must first be converted to a mass flow.

steps.answer: Q = V × ρ × Cp × ΔT, with V = 2,100 m³/h, ρ = 1.19 kg/m³, Cp = 0.24 kcal/kg °C.
steps.explain: Each term converts the volume flow into a heat quantity per hour.

steps.explain: Only the drop from inlet to exit temperature can be recovered.

steps.explain: Cp is given per kg, so the flow must be in kg/h.

steps.prompt: Multiply mass flow × Cp × ΔT.
steps.explain: This is the heat available per hour for recovery.

explain: The book uses the rule of 1% fuel reduction for every 22 °C reduction in flue gas temperature. This is a rule-of-thumb estimate, not a design calculation.

steps.answer: 1% fuel reduction for every 22 °C reduction in flue gas temperature.

steps.explain: Each 22 °C of drop gives 1% of fuel.

front: For a waste heat source that is a vapour stream, what extra heat becomes recoverable?
back: When the vapour is condensed, its latent heat is also recoverable, in addition to its sensible heat.
explain: Latent heat is released at a constant temperature during condensation. For steam or vapour streams it can be a large share of the total heat content.

front: When is heat lost in providing chilled water a high-grade waste heat source?
back: High grade if it can be used to reduce the demand for refrigeration. Low grade if the refrigeration unit is used as a form of heat pump.
explain: The grade depends on whether the recovered heat reduces refrigeration load or only provides low-temperature heat. The book classes this source in Table 8.1.

front: What are the typical waste gas temperature ranges of a glass melting furnace and of a dry-process cement kiln?
back: Glass melting furnace: 1000–1550 °C. Dry-process cement kiln: 620–730 °C.
explain: Both are high-temperature sources in the book's Table 8.2. The high-temperature range is where heat recovery usually gives the most valuable heat.

front: What are the typical exhaust temperature ranges of steam boilers and gas turbines in the medium-temperature band?
back: Steam boiler exhausts: 230–480 °C. Gas turbine exhausts: 370–540 °C.
explain: The book's Table 8.3 lists these as medium-temperature sources. Recovery here usually means steam generation or air heating.

front: True or false: a turbocharged reciprocating engine has a higher exhaust temperature range than a non-turbocharged one?
back: False. Turbocharged: 230–370 °C. Non-turbocharged: 315–600 °C.
explain: The book's Table 8.3 gives both ranges, and the turbocharged range is the lower one. Check these values against the table when answering trap questions.

front: What are the two categories of benefit from waste heat recovery?
back: Direct benefits: lower utility consumption and cost, and lower process cost, because process efficiency improves. Indirect benefits: reduced pollution, smaller equipment sizes, and lower auxiliary energy use.
explain: Direct benefits show up in the energy and process cost lines. Indirect benefits come from a smaller flue gas flow, which allows smaller fans, pumps and other equipment.

front: Which combustible wastes can be burnt in incinerators to recover heat and reduce pollution?
back: Carbon monoxide gas, sour gas, carbon black off-gases, oil sludge, acrylonitrile and other plastic chemicals.
explain: Burning these wastes in incinerators serves two purposes: the heat is recovered, and the release of toxic material to the atmosphere is reduced.

front: Which plant documents should be reviewed to understand a process before designing a waste heat recovery system?
back: Process flow sheets, layout diagrams, piping isometrics, and electrical and instrumentation cable ducting drawings.
explain: This review identifies sources and uses of waste heat, upset conditions caused by recovery, available space, and constraints such as dew point in equipment.

front: Name the economic parameters used to evaluate a waste heat recovery system.
back: Investment, depreciation, payback period and rate of return. Advice from experienced consultants and suppliers should also be obtained.
explain: The economic evaluation supports the choice of system. The book stresses that consultant and supplier advice is needed for a rational decision.

front: Why do recuperators often use parallel flow rather than the more efficient counterflow arrangement?
back: Because the recuperator also cools the exhaust duct that carries the gases away, which extends that duct's service life.
explain: Counterflow would transfer heat more efficiently. Parallel flow is kept because it keeps the duct wall cooler.

front: Why is the metallic concentric-tube recuperator called a 'radiation' recuperator?
back: A substantial part of the heat passing from the hot gases to the inner tube is transferred by radiation. The cold air in the annulus is almost transparent to infrared, so it is heated only by convection.
explain: The hot gas flows in the inner tube and the combustion air flows in the outer annulus. Only the radiant part of the transfer depends on the gas side being hot.

front: How do baffles change a tube-type (convective) recuperator?
back: Baffles make the air pass over the hot tubes more than once: two baffles give a three-pass recuperator, and one baffle giving two passes is a two-pass design. Baffling raises effectiveness but also raises cost and the pressure drop in the combustion air path.
explain: More passes give a larger effective heat transfer area and better effectiveness. The trade-off is extra cost and extra resistance to air flow.

front: Why are shell-and-tube recuperators more compact and more effective than radiation recuperators?
back: They provide a larger heat transfer area through multiple tubes and multiple gas passes.
explain: The book says shell and tube type recuperators are generally more compact and have higher effectiveness. This is why they are used where space and efficiency matter.

front: What temperature limits do ceramic recuperators allow on the gas side and on the preheated air side?
back: Gas side up to 1550 °C; preheated air side up to 815 °C. Metal recuperator liners lose life at inlet temperatures above about 1100 °C.
explain: Ceramic tube recuperators were developed to overcome the temperature limit of metal recuperators. Later designs use short silicon carbide tubes joined by flexible seals.

front: What happens to regenerator performance if the time between reversals is made very long?
back: Thermal storage must be larger, which raises cost. The average preheat temperature is lower, which reduces fuel economy.
explain: Regenerators are widely used in glass and steel melting furnaces for large capacities. The reversal period is a key design choice, balancing storage cost against preheat temperature.

front: What sensible heat transfer efficiency can a heat wheel reach, and how large have heat wheels been built?
back: Up to 85%. Heat wheels have been built up to 21 m in diameter with air capacities up to 1130 m³/min.
explain: A heat wheel is a rotating porous disk with high heat capacity that carries heat from the hot duct to the cold duct. It suits low to medium temperature recovery.

front: What are the three elements of a heat pipe?
back: A sealed container, a capillary wick structure fused to the inner surface of the tube, and a working fluid.
explain: The wick is sealed under vacuum with the working fluid. It returns the condensed liquid to the evaporator region.

front: How does a heat pipe move heat from the hot end to the cold end?
back: At the hot end the working fluid evaporates and absorbs latent heat. The vapour travels to the cool end, condenses and gives up its latent heat. The liquid then flows back through the wick.
explain: The heat pipe has no moving parts and needs no input power. Heat transfer depends on repeated evaporation and condensation of the working fluid.

front: What operating temperature and heat recovery capability do heat pipe heat exchangers offer?
back: They can operate at 315 °C with 60% to 80% heat recovery.
explain: The book also notes that heat pipe systems are lightweight and compact. They lower fan horsepower and need no cooling water or lubrication systems.

front: A heat pipe can transfer up to how many times more thermal energy than copper, the best known conductor?
back: Up to 100 times.
explain: Heat pipes absorb and transfer thermal energy with no moving parts, so they need minimal maintenance.

front: By how much does each 22 °C reduction in flue gas temperature reduce boiler fuel use?
back: About 1% of the boiler's fuel.
explain: This applies whether the heat goes to an economiser (feed water) or an air preheater (combustion air). The book uses it as the standard rule of thumb for boiler heat recovery.

front: How much feed water temperature rise in an economiser, and how much combustion air temperature rise in an air preheater, gives 1% boiler fuel saving?
back: 6 °C rise in feed water temperature, or 20 °C rise in combustion air temperature, gives 1% fuel saving.
explain: These are the book's conversion figures for boiler heat recovery. They make it easy to estimate the saving from a measured temperature change.

front: When must a shell-and-tube heat exchanger be used for waste heat recovery?
back: When the waste heat medium is a liquid or vapour that heats another liquid, because both paths must be sealed to contain their pressures. A condensing vapour is normally kept in the shell.
explain: The higher-pressure fluid is circulated in the tubes, since the shell is inherently weaker. Vapour condensing inside small parallel tubes causes flow instability, so it is placed in the shell.

front: Why is a plate heat exchanger used when the temperature difference is small?
back: When temperature differences are small, the cost of heat exchange surface is a major factor. Thin corrugated plates separated by gaskets give a large surface in a compact unit. Typical uses are milk pasteurisation and food evaporation.
explain: The hot and cold streams flow in alternate channels between the plates. The corrugations improve heat transfer.

front: What is a waste heat boiler, and how does it produce steam?
back: It is usually a water-tube boiler in which hot exhaust gases from gas turbines, incinerators and similar sources pass over water-filled tubes. The water is vaporised in the tubes and the steam is collected in a steam drum.
explain: Because the exhaust gases are usually in the medium-temperature range, the water tubes are often finned to increase the gas-side heat transfer area and make the boiler compact.

front: What is the rule-of-thumb temperature limit for waste heat recovery, and why?
back: Below about 120 °C (or better, 150 °C, for a safe margin) is usually the limit, because of the risk of condensation of corrosive liquids.
explain: Rising fuel costs can make even low-temperature heat worth using for space heating. The corrosion risk sets the practical floor for recovery.

front: Describe the four steps of the vapour compression heat pump cycle.
back: 1) The evaporator extracts heat from the waste heat source and boils the working fluid. 2) The compressor raises its pressure and temperature, using external work. 3) The condenser delivers heat to the user. 4) The throttling valve reduces the pressure back to the evaporator condition, and the cycle repeats.
explain: It is a closed cycle: the circulating substance is kept separate from the source and user streams and reused each time round.

front: How much heat can a heat pump upgrade, relative to the energy the device consumes?
back: More than twice the energy consumed by the device.
explain: A heat pump lifts low-grade heat from ambient air, water or earth to a useful temperature by doing compression work with an electric motor-driven compressor.

front: Why are heat pump applications most promising when both heating and cooling are used?
back: Example: in a plastics factory, chilled water from the heat pump cools the injection moulding machines, while the heat output warms the factory or office.
explain: Using both outputs makes the heat pump's cost go further. The book also lists product drying and maintaining dry storage atmospheres as applications.

front: What is a direct contact heat exchanger, and where is it typically used?
back: Low pressure steam is condensed directly in incoming water, which is sprayed over trays or packed beds, heating it. The typical application is the deaerator of a steam generating station.
explain: Direct contact works only where the steam and water are miscible, as the book notes. The steam is completely condensed in the incoming water.

front: A crude oil furnace heats 500 m³/h of crude (SG 0.85, Cp 0.6 kcal/kg °C) from 255 °C to 360 °C, firing 3.4 t/h of fuel oil with GCV 9,850 kcal/kg. An air preheater heats 57 t/h of combustion air (Cp 0.24) from 28 °C to 195 °C. What is furnace efficiency before and after the air preheater?
back: Before: 80%. After: 85.8%.
explain: The air preheater returns heat to the furnace, so less fuel is needed for the same heat gain in the crude. The heat gain by the crude does not change; only the heat input falls.

steps.explain: Volume (m³) × 1000 × SG gives mass in kg/h.

steps.prompt: Find the heat input before the air preheater.
steps.explain: Fuel in t/h is converted to kg/h and multiplied by GCV.

steps.prompt: Find the furnace efficiency before the air preheater.
steps.explain: Efficiency is heat gain divided by heat input.

steps.prompt: Find the heat recovered by the air preheater.
steps.explain: Air is heated from the 28 °C ambient, not from zero.

steps.prompt: Find the new heat input and the efficiency after the air preheater.
steps.explain: The heat saved from the flue gas reduces the fuel input for the same heat gain.

front: A boiler economiser cuts flue gas temperature from 260 °C to 150 °C. Using the book's rule, what is the fuel saving?
back: About 5% of boiler fuel.

front: What are the three ways heat flows from a warm medium to a cooler one?
back: Radiation (warm surface to a cooler surface across an air space), conduction (through solid or fluid materials) and convection (by physical movement of air).
explain: Heat transfer is the flow of thermal energy from a hotter object to a cooler one. Radiation needs no medium, conduction moves heat through material without bulk movement, and convection carries heat along with moving air or fluid.

front: What four criteria govern the rate of heat transfer between a hot and a cold fluid?
back: (1) Temperature difference between the fluids; (2) area of the conductive barrier; (3) resistance to heat flow in each fluid; (4) material of the barrier, which must be compatible with the process fluids and must not corrode or contaminate them.
explain: A larger temperature difference and a larger area both raise the heat flow. High resistance on either fluid side slows the overall rate, so the barrier material is chosen for compatibility as well as conductivity.

front: What is a heat exchanger?
back: A device that transfers heat energy from one fluid to another, generally without mixing the two fluids.
explain: Heat only flows from hotter to cooler, so the two fluids must be at different temperatures and in thermal contact. They stay separate, which is why the design uses walls or tubes between them.

front: Name the five purposes a heat exchanger can serve.
back: (1) Heat a cooler fluid with a hotter one; (2) cool a hot fluid with a cooler one; (3) boil a liquid with a hotter fluid; (4) condense a gas with a cooler fluid; (5) boil a liquid while condensing a hotter gas.
explain: The purposes cover sensible heating or cooling and phase change. Recognising the purpose tells you whether the exchange is sensible, latent or both.

front: Is the heat lost by the hot fluid exactly equal to the heat gained by the cold fluid in a real heat exchanger?
back: No. In theory they are equal, but environmental heat losses make them differ slightly. Calculations assume they are equal to simplify the work, and insulation keeps the losses small.
explain: The energy balance (heat lost by hot side = heat gained by cold side) is the basis of exchanger calculations. Insulating equipment and piping minimises the losses that the simplification ignores.

front: What does Q = m × Cₚ × ΔT give, and what are its units?
back: Heat transferred Q in kW, where m is mass flow in kg/s, Cₚ is specific heat in kJ/kg·°C and ΔT is the temperature difference between the fluid's inlet and outlet in °C.
explain: This is the sensible heat gained or lost by a fluid with no phase change. Apply it to each stream separately, then use the energy balance to link the hot and cold sides.

front: What is the basic heat exchanger design equation?
back: Q = U × A × ΔT_LMTD, where Q is the heat transfer rate, U the overall heat transfer coefficient, A the heat transfer surface area and ΔT_LMTD the log mean temperature difference.
explain: The equation links the heat duty to the driving force and the surface. For a known duty, a higher U or a higher ΔT_LMTD means less area is needed. It can be rearranged to size the area.

front: What LMTD value is used when the temperature difference between the two fluids is the same at both ends of the exchanger?
back: The log mean formula gives zero in this case, so the LMTD is taken as the temperature difference at each end (the terminal temperature difference). In the book's example that is 30 °C.
explain: When the temperature difference is constant along the length, the log formula breaks down. Using the terminal difference keeps the design equation usable.

front: What does the overall heat transfer coefficient U depend on?
back: The conductivity of the wall separating the fluids, the convection coefficients on the hot and cold sides, the wall thickness and the fouling coefficients. In practice U is often found by measuring the other parameters and calculating it.
explain: U combines all the resistances between the two fluids. Fouling deposits add resistance, so they lower U.

front: Between what limits does the temperature correction factor F usually lie, and when can F be taken as 1?
back: F usually lies between 0.85 and 0.98. F can be taken as 1 only when the flow is purely counter-current.
explain: F corrects the LMTD for exchangers that are not truly counter-current, which is common in cross-flow and multi-pass designs. Charts or a numerical method are used to find F for a given configuration.

front: What are the three broad flow-pattern classes of heat exchangers?
back: Counter flow, parallel flow and cross flow.
explain: The classes describe how the hot and cold fluids move relative to each other. Flow pattern, along with available space and economics, sets the type and configuration of an exchanger.

front: When is a counter-flow design most valuable?
back: When there is a temperature cross, meaning the desired outlet temperature of one fluid lies between the inlet and outlet temperatures of the other fluid.
explain: In counter flow the hottest cold-side outlet meets the hottest hot-side inlet, so the cold fluid can be heated above the hot fluid's outlet temperature. A true counter flow is hard to build for many applications, but plate, double-pipe and spiral exchangers come close.

front: Where are cross-flow designs commonly used, and why?
back: In most shell-and-tube and air-cooled exchangers, because a counter-flow layout is sometimes impractical due to high flow volumes or space restrictions.
explain: In cross flow the two fluids move at right angles. Most applications use multiple passes, which combine cross flow and counter flow and can produce a partial temperature cross.

front: What is a double-pipe heat exchanger and where is it used?
back: Two concentric tubes, with one fluid in the inner tube and the other in the annular space between the tubes. It is used for cooling process fluids where only small heat transfer areas are needed.
explain: It is one of the simplest configurations. It can run in parallel or counter flow, and several units can be combined in series or parallel to form a system.

front: In a shell-and-tube exchanger, why is the process fluid usually placed inside the tubes?
back: For ease of cleaning, and to use the higher pressure capability inside the tubes.
explain: Tubes handle higher pressure better than the shell, and the tube side is easier to clean. Baffles on the shell side direct the flow across the tubes and support them.

front: What are the main advantages and the main limitation of plate heat exchangers?
back: Advantages: high heat transfer coefficients and area, low pressure drop and very high effectiveness. Limitation: relatively low pressure capability.
explain: Corrugated plates increase turbulence and heat transfer. Plate exchangers suit duties with modest pressure where high effectiveness is needed.

front: How does the overall heat transfer coefficient of a plate exchanger compare with a traditional shell-and-tube exchanger?
back: Plate exchangers can reach about 8,000 W/m²·°C under favourable conditions. Traditional shell-and-tube exchangers are usually below 2,500 W/m²·°C.
explain: The much higher U of plate units means a smaller area for the same duty. This is one reason plate units suit close temperature approaches.

front: Why is counter flow usually preferred, and when is parallel flow chosen instead?
back: Counter flow gives a larger effective LMTD, so a smaller area and greater potential energy recovery. Parallel flow is chosen for a high initial heating rate, for moderate tube wall temperatures (useful where fouling is aggravated by high temperature) or for rapid heating of viscous fluids.
explain: A larger LMTD means less area for the same heat transfer. Parallel flow gives cooler tube walls and a fast start, which can cut pumping needs for viscous fluids.

front: How do surface condensers differ from barometric condensers?
back: Surface condensers circulate cooling water through tubes, so steam condenses on a cool surface and the condensate is collected. Barometric condensers rely on direct contact between the cooling water and the steam.
explain: Surface condensers keep the condensate separate from the cooling water, so it can be returned and reused. Barometric units are simpler but mix the cooling water with the steam.

front: What is the role of a condenser in a steam turbine or ejector system?
back: In turbine applications it runs under vacuum and removes a significant amount of latent heat from the exhaust steam, which is recovered as condensate. In ejector applications it condenses the motive steam and condensable vapours, reducing the motive steam needed.
explain: Recovering the condensate returns hot water to the system instead of losing it. In ejector systems, condensing the motive steam cuts the steam the ejector consumes.

front: Why is steam injected into the bottom of a distillation tower?
back: To reduce the partial pressures of the hydrocarbons, which facilitates their separation and reduces coke formation on tray surfaces.
explain: Distillation separates crude oil or feedstock into components by their boiling points. The lower partial pressure helps the components separate, and it also reduces coking on the trays.

front: What does an evaporator do and how is it usually built?
back: It reduces the water content of a liquid, usually by heating it with steam, to concentrate the product. Most are shell-and-tube exchangers with steam on the shell side and the product being concentrated in the tubes.
explain: Evaporators are used widely in food processing, chemicals, steel, forest products and textiles. They can be single-effect or multiple-effect.

front: Roughly what fraction of the steam of a single-effect evaporator is needed after adding a first effect, and then a second effect?
back: Adding one effect cuts steam use to nearly 50% of the original. Adding another effect brings it to nearly 33%.
explain: Each effect reuses the latent heat of the vapour from the previous effect. The savings drop off with each added effect, which is why the number of effects is limited.

front: Why does reduced heat transfer in an exchanger matter for a process?
back: It almost always affects cycle time and product cost. Exchanger performance should be monitored and maintained at regular intervals set by cost-benefit criteria.
explain: Efficient heating and cooling depend on good heat transfer from the surfaces. A good operation and maintenance policy starts at installation and continues in later years.

front: What happens to utility requirements and to exchanger area when the minimum approach temperature (ΔTmin) in pinch analysis is increased?
back: Utility requirements (steam and cooling) increase, and area requirements decrease.
explain: A larger ΔTmin means less heat is recovered, so more hot and cold utility is needed. A larger approach temperature also means the exchangers can be smaller.

front: In pinch analysis, what is the defining parameter that decides whether a hot and cold stream match is suitable?
back: Quality, which for heat means temperature.
explain: Pinch treats a process as supplies and demands of commodities such as energy or water. Inefficient transfer between mismatched streams wastes the imported utility.

front: What do the hot and cold composite curves show in pinch analysis?
back: The hot composite curve shows the process's heat availability and the cold composite curve shows its heat demands. The degree to which they overlap is the potential for heat recovery.
explain: Building the curves needs a complete and consistent heat and mass balance. Sliding one curve horizontally changes only the relative position, not the stream data.

front: In the chapter's composite-curve example with ΔTmin = 10 °C, what are the minimum hot and cold utility loads?
back: Minimum hot utility Q_Hmin = 900 kW. Minimum cold utility Q_Cmin = 750 kW.
explain: The heating and cooling that remain after maximum internal recovery between the composite curves give these targets. They set the energy target before any heat exchanger is designed.

front: What is the main advantage of pinch technology over conventional design methods?
back: It sets energy and capital cost targets for a process or a whole site before design, so the scope for energy savings and the investment needed can be judged before projects are identified.
explain: Targets come from stream data alone. Pinch also guides debottlenecking, choice of combined heat and power, and recovery of low-grade waste heat.

front: For a given heat duty and temperature difference, does a higher heat transfer coefficient need a larger or a smaller area?
back: A smaller area. From A = Q / (U × ΔT_LMTD), a higher U reduces A.
explain: A higher U means heat passes through the wall more readily, so less surface is needed. This is why high-U plate exchangers can be compact.

front: Does an exchanger's effectiveness depend on the LMTD?
back: No. Effectiveness is the ratio of the actual heat transferred to the heat that an exchanger of infinite size could transfer. It is built from the flow heat capacities and inlet temperatures, not the LMTD.
explain: Effectiveness is the best way to compare different types of exchanger. The LMTD is an average temperature difference used in the design equation and is not part of the effectiveness definition.
